clusters.cluster_name: Creatine: dosing, safety, myths, strength gains

topics.title: Creatine 101: what it is and why it works
topics.angle: The most-studied sports supplement, explained. What creatine does in your muscle, why it helps strength/power, and why you don't need the fancy forms.
numbered_points_outline: 1. MECHANISM — Phosphocreatine shuttles ATP during short high-intensity sets; mechanism of action in the ATP-PC system
2. EVIDENCE — Meta-analyses show consistent small-to-moderate strength + hypertrophy effect (Burke 2023; Desai 2024)
3. MONOHYDRATE IS THE GOLD STANDARD — Cheapest, most researched, no superior alternative form
4. SAFETY — Long-term use is safe in healthy adults; no kidney or liver harm signal in controlled trials
5. WHO SHOULD TAKE IT — Any lifter looking for more work capacity and strength; works regardless of training style

suggested_citations.title: The Effects of Creatine Supplementation Combined with Resistance Training on Regional Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis

topics.title: Creatine dosing: you don't need to load
topics.angle: Mythbust the 20g/day loading protocol. 3-5g daily gets you to the same saturation in ~28 days with less GI upset.
numbered_points_outline: 1. WHAT LOADING DOES — Fills muscle stores faster (~5-7 days) vs the slow path (~28 days)
2. THE ENDPOINT IS THE SAME — Both protocols converge on identical muscle creatine saturation
3. DOSE — 3-5g/day is sufficient for the average lifter; larger athletes may benefit from 5-10g/day per recent dose-response work
4. TIMING — With carbs/protein post-workout shows a small edge but daily consistency is the dominant variable
5. LOADING-SPECIFIC DOWNSIDES — GI upset and water-weight spike; safe but unpleasant for some

topics.title: Creatine and kidneys: the myth that won't die
topics.angle: The 'creatine hurts your kidneys' claim comes from one misread serum creatinine number. Here's what the actual kidney-function data says.
numbered_points_outline: 1. MYTH: Creatine raises serum creatinine / FACT: It raises creatinine (the waste product) because you have more creatine in your body — not because kidneys are damaged
2. MYTH: Long-term use is unsafe / FACT: Position stands and meta-analyses over >20 years show no adverse kidney markers in healthy adults
3. MYTH: You need kidney 'breaks' / FACT: Continuous daily use is the most-studied protocol; no evidence cycling is necessary
4. WHO SHOULD BE CAUTIOUS — Anyone with pre-existing kidney disease should clear supplementation with their doctor; healthy adults are not the audience for that warning
5. THE BOTTOM LINE — Decades of data support safety; a single elevated serum creatinine reading is not kidney damage

suggested_citations.title: The Effects of Creatine Supplementation Combined with Resistance Training on Regional Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis

safety_flags: mention pre-existing kidney disease as the only caveat

topics.title: Creatine for women: same effect, different myth
topics.angle: Women respond to creatine the same way men do. The 'bulky water weight' and 'just for men' claims are wrong.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE EVIDENCE BASE — Meta-analyses include mixed-sex cohorts; women show comparable strength and lean-mass responses
2. WATER WEIGHT IS INTRACELLULAR — 1-2kg water gain sits inside muscle cells, not under the skin; nothing like a 'puffy' look
3. DOSE — Same 3-5g/day; no evidence women need to dose lower
4. BONE HEALTH — Some evidence creatine + resistance training benefits bone density in post-menopausal women
5. CYCLE CONSIDERATIONS — No evidence menstrual cycle requires protocol changes

topics.title: Creatine timing: pre-workout, post-workout, or does it matter?
topics.angle: Timing debates aside, daily consistency is the dominant variable. The post-workout edge is small and may not matter for most lifters.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE CLAIM — Post-workout + carbs/protein shows a small edge in some trials
2. THE REAL DRIVER — Daily total dose and duration matter much more than time of day
3. WHAT IF YOU MISS A DAY — The muscle stores deplete slowly; one missed day is not consequential
4. STACK IT WITH YOUR MEAL — Pair with any protein-containing meal for convenience
5. TRAINING DAY VS REST DAY — Same dose every day; no need to skip non-training days

clusters.cluster_name: Pre-workouts and stimulants + supplement risk (caffeine, beta-alanine, SARMs)

topics.title: Caffeine for strength: the dose that actually works
topics.angle: Meta-analyses pin the minimum ergogenic dose for resistance exercise. Here's the range, the timing, and why more isn't better.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE DOSE — ~3-6 mg/kg bodyweight is the evidence-supported range for strength/power outcomes
2. MINIMUM EFFECTIVE DOSE — Grgic 2022 meta-analysis shows ergogenic effects starting at lower doses than previously thought
3. TIMING — 45-60 min pre-training; peak plasma concentration aligns with the session
4. VELOCITY EFFECTS — Acute caffeine improves movement velocity in resistance exercise per Raya-González 2020 meta
5. WHO RESPONDS BEST — Non-habitual users see the largest effects; tolerance blunts but doesn't eliminate benefits

topics.title: Caffeine and sleep: the 6-hour rule
topics.angle: Caffeine's half-life is 5-7 hours. A 3pm coffee can still be in your system at bedtime. Here's how to get the training boost without wrecking sleep.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE HALF-LIFE — 5-7 hours in most adults; twice that in slow metabolizers
2. THE SLEEP COST — Even when you fall asleep, deep sleep and REM are reduced by evening caffeine
3. TRAINING TIMING DECISION — If you train after 4pm, decaf options or lower doses
4. TOLERANCE DOES NOT EQUAL NO EFFECT — Habitual users still get adenosine blockade even if they feel fine
5. PRACTICAL RULE — Last dose ~8 hours before bedtime for most people

topics.title: Does beta-alanine help powerlifters? (Not really)
topics.angle: Beta-alanine shines for 60-240 second efforts. Powerlifting is 1-3 second efforts. Here's why it mostly doesn't help the big 3 and where it does matter (accessories, hypertrophy blocks).
numbered_points_outline: 1. MECHANISM RECAP — Carnosine buffers H+ ions in high-intensity efforts lasting 60-240s
2. EFFECT SIZE BY DURATION — Saunders 2017 meta shows benefits largely in the minute-plus range
3. POWERLIFTING SPECIFICITY — Single-rep squat/bench/DL takes <5 seconds; not the right energy system
4. WHEN IT HELPS POWERLIFTERS — High-volume accessory work, hypertrophy blocks, 8-15 rep ranges
5. THE HONEST TAKE — Useful for the right training phase, not a universal 'pre-workout must'

topics.title: SARMs: what the FDA and WADA actually say
topics.angle: SARMs are not FDA-approved, are prohibited in sport, and carry documented liver-toxicity risk. This is a safety post, not a 'is the evidence mixed' post.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE FDA POSITION — SARMs are not approved for any human use; marketing them as dietary supplements is illegal
2. THE WADA POSITION — SARMs are on the Prohibited List under S1 (anabolic agents), banned in and out of competition
3. DOCUMENTED HARMS — Clinical literature reports hepatotoxicity, lipid derangements, and cardiovascular adverse events
4. CONTAMINATION RISK — Products sold online frequently contain undeclared SARMs, stimulants, or steroids — tested-athlete programs see repeated positive contamination events
5. WHAT TO DO INSTEAD — Creatine, caffeine, and progressive overload are the evidence-based alternatives; none of them are banned

topics.title: Why you can't trust pre-workout labels
topics.angle: Proprietary blends hide doses, contamination is real, and most pre-workouts under-dose the only ingredients that work. What to look for instead.
numbered_points_outline: 1. PROPRIETARY BLENDS — 'Proprietary blend' means the label hides how much of each ingredient you're getting
2. THE UNDER-DOSING PROBLEM — Beta-alanine at 1.6g, citrulline at 3g, caffeine at 150mg — most products are below effective doses
3. CONTAMINATION RISK — Industry testing has repeatedly found undeclared stimulants and banned substances in supplements
4. WHAT TO LOOK FOR — Informed Sport or NSF Certified for Sport marks, clear mg amounts for each ingredient, no 'blend' labels
5. THE DIY ALTERNATIVE — Separate creatine + caffeine + beta-alanine is cheaper and you control the dose

topics.title: RPE/RIR: what the numbers actually mean
topics.angle: RPE 8 is not 'hard'. It's 'two reps left in the tank'. Calibrating the scale to reality is the whole skill.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE SCALE — RPE 10 = absolute failure; RPE 9 = 1 rep left; RPE 8 = 2 reps left; RPE 7 = 3 reps left; RPE 6 = 4+ reps left
2. WHY IT WORKS — Lets you adjust load day-to-day based on how you're recovering, without abandoning the plan
3. THE CALIBRATION PROBLEM — Most lifters overestimate RPE at moderate loads and underestimate near failure
4. HOW TO TRAIN THE SKILL — Compare predicted vs actual reps-to-failure on the last set of a session once per week
5. WHEN TO USE RPE — Main lifts benefit most; machines and isolation work fine with fixed reps

suggested_citations.title: The Importance of Muscular Strength: Training Considerations

topics.title: Autoregulation: when to override the plan
topics.angle: The whole point of RPE-based programming is flexibility on bad days. Here's the decision tree for when to push, hold, or cut a session.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE TEST SET — First working set tells you the day's capacity; compare to expected
2. IF YOU'RE UNDER — Cap volume, not intensity; finish the heavy work, cut back-off sets
3. IF YOU'RE OVER — Don't chase PRs unless the program calls for it; the plan's top set is the plan's top set
4. THE NEVER-OVERRIDE RULES — Don't override on peaking weeks, meet prep, or first session after a deload
5. TRACKING — Log actual RPE vs planned; patterns show up over 4-8 weeks

suggested_citations.title: Periodization and Block Periodization in Sports: Emphasis on Strength-Power Training — A Provocative and Challenging Narrative

topics.title: Estimated 1RM: using it without abusing it
topics.angle: e1RM from rep-max tests is a great progress tool and a terrible peaking tool. Here's how to use it right.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE MATH — Epley, Brzycki, and RPE-chart based e1RMs diverge at heavy loads and high RPEs
2. WHAT IT'S GOOD FOR — Tracking block-over-block progress at submaximal loads without regularly maxing out
3. WHAT IT'S BAD FOR — Predicting your actual competition max; the error bars widen at true 1RM intensity
4. HOW OFTEN TO TEST — Every 4-8 weeks or at block transitions; not every session
5. LIMITATIONS — Not useful for ~3RM+ with huge grinders where technique degrades

suggested_citations.title: The Minimum Effective Training Dose Required to Increase 1RM Strength in Resistance-Trained Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

clusters.cluster_name: Programming & periodization: volume, intensity, frequency, DUP vs linear

topics.title: The J-shaped volume curve: when more stops working
topics.angle: 10-15 sets/muscle/week is a good floor. Past ~20 sets gains flatten and recovery cost rises. The J curve explained.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE FLOOR — Evidence supports ~10 sets/muscle/week as a productive lower bound for trained lifters
2. THE RISING PART — 10 to ~20 sets/muscle/week shows continued gains for most lifters
3. THE PLATEAU — Beyond ~20 sets diminishing returns kick in, and recovery cost grows
4. INDIVIDUAL VARIANCE — Genetic, training-age, and recovery differences shift the curve
5. HOW TO APPLY — Start at the floor; add 1-2 sets/muscle/week per mesocycle; track performance not soreness

topics.title: Frequency vs volume: does 2x/week beat 4x/week?
topics.angle: When weekly set volume is matched, frequency effects on hypertrophy are small. Pick the frequency you can recover from.
numbered_points_outline: 1. MYTH: HIGHER FREQUENCY IS ALWAYS BETTER / FACT: Matched-volume research shows near-equivalence
2. WHY SOME LIFTERS SWEAR BY HIGH FREQUENCY — It spreads fatigue and lets them handle more total volume
3. WHY SOME LIFTERS SWEAR BY LOW FREQUENCY — Fewer heavy sessions, more recovery between them
4. THE DECISION — Training age, recovery, schedule; not 'the science says X'
5. PROGRAMMING — 2-4x/week/muscle is the productive range; pick what fits your life

topics.title: DUP vs linear periodization: what the research actually shows
topics.angle: Undulating periodization isn't a magic bullet. For trained lifters the differences are small; for intermediates DUP may have a modest edge.
numbered_points_outline: 1. LINEAR — Progressive intensity week-over-week, volume decreases; simple, works for beginners
2. DUP — Intensity and rep ranges vary within a week (e.g. heavy Mon, moderate Wed, light Fri)
3. EVIDENCE — Head-to-head trials show small effects in either direction; not a settled superiority
4. WHO BENEFITS FROM DUP — Intermediates plateaued on linear; people who get bored easily and need variation for adherence
5. WHO DOESN'T — Absolute beginners (linear is simpler), meet-prep lifters (block periodization wins here)

topics.title: The minimum effective dose for strength gains
topics.angle: You don't need 20 sets per muscle. Androulakis-Korakakis et al. pinned the lower bound. Here it is.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE META — Androulakis-Korakakis 2020 found meaningful 1RM strength gains with very low weekly volume
2. THE NUMBER — As little as ~4 heavy sets per lift per week produces measurable strength progress in trained men
3. WHAT IT DOESN'T PIN — Hypertrophy response needs more volume than strength
4. WHY IT MATTERS — Time-constrained lifters can train productively with much less than the 'standard' prescription
5. HOW TO USE IT — Default to more; pull back to the MED during busy life phases without abandoning the gym

The Minimum Effective Training Dose Required for 1RM Strength in Powerlifters

topics.title: Block periodization for powerlifters: the basic template
topics.angle: Accumulation → transmutation → realization. A walkthrough of the block structure that coaches world-record totals.
numbered_points_outline: PHASE 1 — ACCUMULATION: High volume, moderate intensity (RPE 6-8), 3-5 weeks; drives hypertrophy and work capacity
PHASE 2 — TRANSMUTATION: Moderate volume, higher intensity (RPE 7-9), 3-4 weeks; converts new muscle to strength
PHASE 3 — REALIZATION (PEAK): Low volume, top-end intensity (RPE 8-10), 2-3 weeks; primes nervous system for maximal output
THE DELOAD — 4-7 day recovery block after realization; ~50% volume reduction
THE MISTAKE TO AVOID — Running accumulation intensities during realization or vice versa; each phase needs its own stimulus

clusters.cluster_name: Protein & macros: g/kg targets, quality, distribution

topics.title: The 1.62 g/kg protein ceiling: where gains plateau
topics.angle: The Morton 2018 meta-analysis pinned the ceiling of additional strength/hypertrophy from dietary protein. More than ~1.62 g/kg/day stops producing additional gains.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE FINDING — Morton et al. 2018: benefits plateau at ~1.62 g/kg/day for lean-mass and strength outcomes
2. WHAT IT DOESN'T SAY — That more protein is harmful; just that it doesn't add more muscle or strength
3. HOW TO HIT IT — For a 75kg lifter, ~120g/day distributed across 3-4 meals
4. QUALITY STILL MATTERS — Leucine content, digestibility, and amino acid profile shape the response within the target
5. THE BOTTOM LINE — Hit the target, prioritize total daily intake over timing tricks

suggested_citations.title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults

topics.title: The anabolic window: 30 minutes or 3 hours?
topics.angle: The 'slam protein within 30 minutes of lifting' rule is a relic. The actual window is measured in hours, not minutes.
numbered_points_outline: 1. MYTH: 30-MINUTE WINDOW / FACT: Meta-analyses show the post-workout window is ~3+ hours wide
2. WHAT DRIVES THE RESPONSE — Total daily protein and per-meal leucine content, not a narrow clock
3. THE FED STATE MATTERS — If you ate 1-2 hours pre-lift, the 'post-workout window' concern is mostly moot
4. WHO DOES NEED POST-WORKOUT PROTEIN — Fasted trainers, very early morning sessions, athletes going multiple sessions per day
5. THE PRACTICAL RULE — Hit your total daily target; spread it across 3-5 meals; stop stressing the clock

topics.title: Protein distribution: 3 meals vs 6 meals
topics.angle: Eating protein across 3-5 meals is optimal for MPS. More than 5 meals doesn't help; fewer than 3 may cost you.
numbered_points_outline: 1. MPS PULSE — Each high-protein meal triggers ~3-hour muscle protein synthesis pulse
2. THE OPTIMAL RANGE — 3-5 meals/day with 0.4-0.5 g/kg protein each is the research-supported range
3. ONE HUGE MEAL VS SPREAD — Total protein matters most, but very concentrated intake wastes some for MPS
4. PRE-SLEEP PROTEIN — Some evidence a pre-sleep dose (30-40g casein) supports overnight MPS for lifters training hard
5. PRACTICAL PATTERN — Breakfast, lunch, dinner minimum; add pre/post workout or pre-sleep for higher targets

topics.title: Protein quality: whey vs beef vs plant
topics.angle: Whey is the research gold standard but not the only option. Beef protein and plant blends can close the gap if you hit the leucine threshold.
numbered_points_outline: 1. LEUCINE IS THE TRIGGER — ~2.5-3g leucine per meal maximizes MPS signal
2. WHEY — Fast-digesting, leucine-rich, well-studied; the benchmark
3. BEEF PROTEIN ISOLATE — Meta-analysis shows comparable body-composition outcomes when total protein is matched
4. PLANT PROTEIN — Needs higher doses or blended sources (pea + rice) to match whey's leucine hit
5. THE DECISION — Preference, cost, and digestive tolerance; all can work if total daily protein is met

clusters.cluster_name: Technique & equipment optimization: big 3, belting, stance/grip

topics.title: High bar vs low bar squat: which is 'better'?
topics.angle: Neither is universally better. Bar placement changes the moment arms; your levers decide which feels natural.
numbered_points_outline: 1. BAR POSITIONS — High bar sits on the traps; low bar sits on the rear delts, 2-3 inches lower
2. BIOMECHANICAL DIFFERENCE — Low bar shifts load backward, favors hip-drive and forward torso lean
3. WHO PICKS WHAT — Long femurs and strong posterior chain → low bar; shorter femurs + quad dominance → high bar often feels better
4. LOAD DIFFERENCES — Low bar typically allows ~5-10% more load; not a reason to pick it if technique suffers
5. THE COMPETITIVE ANSWER — IPF rules allow either; pick the one your leverages and injuries agree with

suggested_citations.title: Injuries among weightlifters and powerlifters: a systematic review

topics.title: Sumo vs conventional deadlift: biomechanics, not morality
topics.angle: Sumo isn't cheating and conventional isn't purer. Both are legal in every federation; your anthropometry decides which is your strength lift.
numbered_points_outline: 1. RANGE OF MOTION — Sumo has a shorter bar path; conventional uses a longer path but more hip extensor involvement
2. LEVER REALITY — Long arms + short torso favor conventional; short arms + long torso favor sumo
3. MUSCLE RECRUITMENT — Research shows similar total muscle work; different distribution between hips, quads, and back
4. INJURY RATE — Similar between the two styles when matched for training age
5. THE HONEST TAKE — Whichever gives you the higher, more technically consistent lift is yours

suggested_citations.title: Injuries among weightlifters and powerlifters: a systematic review

topics.title: The bench press setup that unlocks leverage
topics.angle: Most missed bench lifts are setup failures, not strength failures. Shoulder retraction, foot drive, and arch change what the bar has to travel.
numbered_points_outline: 1. SHOULDER RETRACTION — Pull shoulder blades down and together, lock them against the bench
2. FOOT DRIVE — Feet planted, legs active; drive pushes you into the bench for stability, not off it
3. ARCH — A moderate thoracic arch shortens the bar path and engages lats; not a lower-back gymnastics display
4. GRIP WIDTH — Most lifters bench too wide; slightly narrower reduces shoulder stress and bar travel
5. WHEN TO BREAK THE RULES — Rehabbing from shoulder injury may mean a less arched setup and wider grip for comfort

suggested_citations.title: Injuries among weightlifters and powerlifters: a systematic review

topics.title: Weightlifting belts: when to wear one
topics.angle: Belts don't replace bracing, they amplify it. Use above ~80% 1RM and learn to brace without one at warmup weights.
numbered_points_outline: 1. WHAT A BELT DOES — Gives your core something to brace against, increasing intra-abdominal pressure
2. WHEN TO USE — Typically above 80% of 1RM on squat and deadlift; lighter work is fine beltless
3. WHEN NOT — Warmups, accessories, and rehab work build the core's ability to brace unassisted
4. BELT-ONLY BRACING IS A TRAP — If you can't brace without a belt, you don't brace with one — you lean on it
5. SIZING — 4-inch lever belts are the gold standard for powerlifters; start tight enough that you can't fit more than two fingers between belt and abs at the top of a breath

topics.title: Cutting without losing strength: the high-protein deficit
topics.angle: A moderate deficit + high protein + resistance training preserves most of your strength. Aggressive cuts compound the losses.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE DEFICIT — 10-20% below maintenance is the sweet spot; deeper cuts accelerate strength loss
2. THE PROTEIN LEVER — Bump to 1.6-2.2 g/kg during the cut; the higher end spares more lean mass
3. THE TRAINING LEVER — Maintain intensity; drop volume as energy intake drops
4. RATE — 0.5-1% bodyweight per week is sustainable for most lifters
5. THE BOTTOM LINE — Slower cuts preserve more strength; aggressive cuts cost you the lifts

topics.title: Lean bulking: the 250-500g/week rule
topics.angle: Aggressive bulks add fat faster than muscle. A ~500 g/week gain is the maximum productive rate for most lifters.
numbered_points_outline: 1. MUSCLE GROWTH HAS A CEILING — Natural lifters gain muscle in grams, not kilograms per week; excess is fat
2. THE NUMBER — 250-500 g/week weight gain is the productive range for most trained lifters
3. NOVICES CAN PUSH HIGHER — Beginners can handle 500-750 g/week without much fat accumulation
4. P-RATIO — The ratio of muscle to fat in newly gained weight depends on training age, recovery, and surplus size
5. THE TRACKING RULE — Weigh in weekly, average over 2 weeks; adjust by ±200 kcal when the trend is off

topics.title: Body recomposition: who it works for
topics.angle: Recomp isn't magic. It works for specific populations — novices, detrained lifters, higher fat mass — and fails for most intermediate/advanced lifters.

4. THE DATA — Evidence supports resistance training + high protein preserving or slowly adding muscle in energy deficit
5. WHAT TO DO IF YOU'RE NOT A NOVICE — Pick a direction (cut or bulk); recomp is usually just slower progress at both

topics.title: The 2-week powerlifting taper: what the research shows
topics.angle: Tapering and peaking review (Travis 2020) lays out the evidence-based framework. Here's a two-week peak template.
numbered_points_outline: WEEK -2 — OPENERS: Squat/bench/deadlift at ~92% of planned opener; volume cut to ~60% of peak block
WEEK -1 — SINGLES: One heavy single per lift at ~95% opener, Tuesday/Wednesday latest
WEEK 0 — MEET WEEK: Light technique work Mon/Tue, full rest Wed-Fri, meet Saturday
THE VOLUME DROP — Volume falls ~40-60% in week -2 and another ~50% in week -1; intensity stays near-max
THE MISTAKE — Adding volume or intensity 'because you feel good'; tapers work by removing stress, not piling it on

topics.title: Meet attempt selection: the 92/97/100+ rule
topics.angle: Opener conservative, second attempt near training top single, third attempt for the PR. The numbers that keep you in the meet.
numbered_points_outline: 1. OPENER — ~92% of training 1RM; a lift you've done 100 times; the point is to go 1/1 not to PR
2. SECOND ATTEMPT — ~97% of training 1RM or your recent heavy single; builds your total
3. THIRD ATTEMPT — PR territory or strategic total-builder; only go here if you went 2/2 and the lift felt right
4. NEVER BOMB — Bombing an opener (missing all 3) = disqualification; your opener discipline is the meet's most important decision
5. FEDERATION CONTEXT — IPF rules may add wrinkles (red light conditions, depth standards) that change what counts as a safe opener

topics.title: The meet-day warmup: from empty bar to opener
topics.angle: A concrete jump-set template for squat/bench/deadlift meet warmups, timed to the flight.
numbered_points_outline: SQUAT JUMPS — Empty bar × 5; 40% × 5; 60% × 3; 75% × 2; 85% × 1; 92% × 1 (opener)
BENCH JUMPS — Similar pattern; 6-8 warmup singles total before opener
DEADLIFT JUMPS — Higher base weight; 4-6 warmup singles (deadlifts are taxing; fewer is better)
TIMING — Final warmup single ~10 minutes before you're called; stay warm without going stale
FLIGHT MATH — Know how many lifters are in your flight; start warmups so your opener lines up with ~4-5 lifters before you

topics.title: Deloads: when to take one and what to do
topics.angle: Planned deloads beat reactive ones. Here are the signals and the template.
numbered_points_outline: 1. WHEN TO DELOAD — Every 4-8 weeks as part of the block, or reactively when performance drops across sessions
2. REACTIVE SIGNALS — Top sets feel heavier than usual for multiple sessions, sleep degrading, recurring small injuries
3. HOW TO DELOAD — Drop volume ~50%, keep intensity ~90% of working loads; not a 'vacation week' from the gym
4. THE MISTAKE — Taking a full week off; you lose adaptation momentum without reducing joint stress more than a light week
5. POST-DELOAD — Return to working loads at the previous block's weights, not a fresh PR attempt

topics.title: Low-back pain while lifting: train through or rest?
topics.angle: Not all pain is injury. Here's the decision framework for back-tweak days: what to modify, what to stop, and when to get help.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE GREEN-LIGHT ZONE — Mild discomfort, no radicular symptoms, returns to baseline within 24h — train with reduced load
2. THE YELLOW-LIGHT ZONE — Pain that changes your movement pattern — stop the aggravating lift, work around it
3. THE RED-LIGHT ZONE — Radiating pain down the leg, numbness, weakness, bladder/bowel changes — stop training, see a clinician
4. THE SQUAT/DEADLIFT SUB — Paused squats at lower load, trap bar or rack pulls, front squats — maintain training without re-loading the injury
5. THE TAPER-BACK — When pain resolves, return to full-range at 70% working weight for 2-3 sessions before normal load

topics.title: The pre-lift meal: what the research actually supports
topics.angle: For most lifters, a moderate protein-carb meal 1-3 hours pre-training covers the evidence base. The rest is personal preference and GI tolerance.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE WINDOW — 1-3 hours before training allows most meals to clear GI tract without hunger mid-session
2. PROTEIN — 20-40g of protein pre-lift overlaps MPS into the session
3. CARBS — Moderate carbs (~0.5-1 g/kg) support performance in longer/higher-volume sessions
4. FAT — Lower fat pre-workout reduces GI issues for most people; it is not harmful, just individual
5. THE PRACTICAL RULE — Same meal, same timing, for 2 weeks before a big session; build a reliable pattern

topics.title: Carbs around training: how much, when?
topics.angle: Strength training runs on glycogen. Carbs pre-lift fuel performance; carbs post-lift refill stores. The numbers matter less than hitting the daily target.
numbered_points_outline: 1. PRE-LIFT CARBS — 0.5-1 g/kg 1-3 hours before training supports work capacity in higher-volume sessions
2. INTRA-LIFT CARBS — Matter only for sessions >60 minutes at high intensity; powerlifting training usually doesn't qualify
3. POST-LIFT CARBS — Don't need a separate 'window'; hit daily total and you've refilled glycogen by the next session
4. DAILY TARGET — 4-7 g/kg for most strength athletes; higher on high-volume days, lower on rest days
5. LOW-CARB LIFTERS — Can still train hard at lower carb intakes but may see performance loss on high-volume days

topics.title: The minimum effective warmup: 5 minutes, not 30
topics.angle: You don't need a 30-minute foam-rolling mobility flow before lifting. 5 min light cardio + a handful of dynamic moves + progressive warmup sets covers the evidence base.
numbered_points_outline: 1. WHY WE WARM UP — Raise muscle temperature, increase synovial flow, activate the patterns you're about to load
2. THE MINIMAL RECIPE — 3-5 min easy bike/row/walk, 3-5 dynamic moves specific to the day's lift, then progressive warmup sets
3. WHAT TO SKIP — Long foam-roll circuits and 10-minute mobility routines aren't required for lifting performance
4. RAMP SETS ARE THE REAL WARMUP — Progressive warmup sets (empty bar → working weight) do most of the neural-prep work
5. WHEN TO DO MORE — Cold-room sessions, post-injury return, or first session of the day after sitting all day warrant a longer ramp

topics.title: Static stretching before lifting: the one thing to stop doing
topics.angle: Long static stretches (>30s) before a heavy session measurably reduce force and power output for that session. Keep static stretching — just do it after, not before.
numbered_points_outline: 1. MYTH: Static stretching prevents injury and primes the muscle / FACT: The acute effect is reduced force and power for that session when holds exceed ~30s
2. MYTH: Dynamic warmups and static stretching are interchangeable / FACT: Dynamic movement prep raises temperature and primes motor patterns without the acute force-reduction downside
3. MYTH: You should never static stretch / FACT: Static stretching has flexibility benefits — do it post-session or on rest days, not immediately before heavy lifts
4. THE EXCEPTION — Holds under ~30s appear to have minimal acute strength impact and are fine if you enjoy them
5. THE PRACTICAL RULE — Dynamic before lifting, static after lifting or on rest days

topics.title: Ramp sets: the real warmup for heavy lifting
topics.angle: Progressive warmup sets are where your nervous system gets ready for heavy work. Here's a ramp template for the main lifts.

4. ADJUST FOR THE LIFT — Deadlifts need fewer ramp reps than squats (more fatigue per rep); bench sits in between
5. THE LAST WARMUP SET — Should feel like a 'heavy but clean' rehearsal for the first working set, not a grind

topics.title: The interference effect: does cardio kill your gains?
topics.angle: The 'cardio kills gains' claim is partially true and mostly overblown. The Huiberts 2024 meta-analysis shows the interference effect is real but sex- and region-specific: strongest for lower-body strength in trained men, minimal elsewhere.
numbered_points_outline: 1. WHAT INTERFERENCE ACTUALLY IS — Adding endurance work can blunt strength/hypertrophy adaptations vs strength training alone
2. IT'S NOT UNIFORM — Huiberts 2024 meta shows the effect is driven mostly by lower-body strength in trained men; upper-body and untrained lifters see little impact
3. VOLUME AND MODALITY MATTER — High-volume running produces more interference than cycling or rowing at matched loads
4. SEPARATION HELPS — Separating strength and endurance sessions by 6+ hours (or different days) reduces interference
5. THE BOTTOM LINE — For most lifters, moderate cardio won't wreck gains; pro/advanced lower-body specialists are the ones who need to manage it carefully

topics.title: Strength first or cardio first? The session-order question
topics.angle: When you have to do both in one session, lift first. Meta-analysis on concurrent-training session ordering shows strength-before-endurance preserves strength adaptations better than the reverse.
numbered_points_outline: 1. THE CLAIM — Acute fatigue from endurance work impairs the neural drive for heavy strength work that follows it
2. THE META-ANALYSIS — Murlasits 2017 reviews trials comparing S→E vs E→S session order; strength-first preserves 1RM adaptations better
3. THE PHYSIOLOGICAL WHY — AMPK activation from endurance may blunt mTOR signaling for hypertrophy when cardio comes first
4. PRACTICAL APPLICATION — If you lift and run on the same day, lift first; if separation is possible, put them 6+ hours apart
5. EXCEPTIONS — If cardio is your primary sport (not strength), the reverse may be appropriate

topics.title: Zone 2 cardio: the cheapest recovery tool you're not using
topics.angle: Low-intensity Zone 2 work (easy bike/walk/row, 60-70% max HR) improves work capacity and recovery between lifting sessions without meaningful interference — if you keep the volume in check.
numbered_points_outline: 1. WHAT ZONE 2 IS — Conversational pace, nasal-breathing if you can, ~60-70% max HR or RPE 4-5/10
2. WHY IT'S USEFUL FOR LIFTERS — Improves between-set recovery, general work capacity, and cardiovascular health without the neural fatigue of HIIT
3. DOSE — 2-3 sessions per week, 20-40 min each is a reasonable starting range for most lifters
4. MODALITY — Bike/row/walk over running if you're worried about lower-body interference (per the Huiberts meta)
5. THE REAL WIN — Better resting HR, better recovery between heavy sessions, and meaningful CV health benefit for a lifetime of lifting

topics.title: Concurrent training for women: the data looks different
topics.angle: The female-specific concurrent-training literature shows women tolerate concurrent training better than men on the interference-effect axis. The Mikkonen 2024 review is the first big synthesis of this evidence.
numbered_points_outline: 1. WHAT THE REVIEW FOUND — Women show less of a strength-adaptation interference signal from added endurance work than men in matched protocols
2. WHY — Hypotheses include slower fatigue recovery in men's type II fibers, sex-linked AMPK/mTOR signaling differences, and baseline training-status differences in the study samples
3. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR PROGRAMMING — Women lifting AND running/cycling can often do both without aggressive session separation
4. STILL NOT FREE — Volume still matters; high-volume endurance work can interfere with strength gains in women too, just less severely
5. THE BOTTOM LINE — Don't apply male-data interference anxiety to female lifters; the evidence base now has its own synthesis

topics.title: HIIT or steady-state: which cardio works with lifting?
topics.angle: HIIT and LISS both have their place alongside strength training. HIIT is time-efficient but shares neural fatigue with heavy lifts; LISS is cheap recovery work. The Kang 2022 meta maps out what HIIT-based concurrent training actually does.
numbered_points_outline: 1. WHAT HIIT DOES IN CONCURRENT TRAINING — Kang 2022 meta finds HIIT-based concurrent programs improve strength/power and aerobic capacity simultaneously in trained team-sport athletes
2. WHAT HIIT COSTS — Neural and muscular fatigue that overlaps with heavy lifting; treat it like a fourth training session, not a recovery tool
3. WHAT LISS DOES — Low-intensity steady state builds aerobic base and recovery capacity with minimal overlap with lifting fatigue
4. HOW TO COMBINE — 1-2 short HIIT sessions + 1-2 LISS sessions per week is a defensible starting point for most strength athletes
5. THE PITFALL — Stacking HIIT days on top of heavy lifting days compounds fatigue and is the most common reason concurrent programs blow up
